title: Global Multi-Channel Notification Platform (50M Events/Day)
businessContext: A global social and banking super-app needs to send 50,000,000 notifications per day across Email (SendGrid), Mobile Push (APNs / FCM), SMS (Twilio), and In-App WebSockets. Users currently complain about duplicate notifications, critical fraud alerts being delayed behind promotional marketing blasts, and lack of quiet-hour preferences.
problemStatement: Design an end-to-end multi-channel notification engine that handles high-throughput ingestion, enforces user notification preferences and quiet hours, deduplicates rapid events, prioritizes critical transactional alerts over marketing campaigns, and handles downstream provider rate limits and failures.
constraints: Throughput: 50M notifications/day (~600 sustained QPS, 5,000 peak QPS).
P99 Latency: < 2 seconds for High-Priority transactional alerts (OTP, fraud, payments).
At-least-once delivery with deduplication window (e.g. 15 minutes for repeated identical events).
Channel rate limiting per user (e.g. max 3 promotional notifications/day).

systemDesignReqs.scale: 50 Million notifications / day, 5k peak writes / sec, 100M active mobile devices.
functional: Send notifications via Push (APNs/FCM), Email, SMS, In-App.
Support priority tiers: P0 (Emergency / OTP), P1 (Account updates), P2 (Social/Marketing).
User preference center (opt-in/opt-out per channel, quiet hours per timezone).
Deduplication and rate limiting per user/channel.
nonFunctional: Fault-tolerant: provider outages must not lose messages.
assumptions: User devices and push tokens are registered in a Device Store.
Downstream vendors (SendGrid, Twilio, APNs) have varying rate limits and occasional latency spikes.

candidateTasks: Architect the system components: API Gateway, Ingestion Service, Message Broker (Kafka / RabbitMQ), Notification Worker Pools, Cache/State Store (Redis), Database (Postgres / DynamoDB).
Define the API contract: `POST /v1/notifications/send` with payload schema.
Explain the Priority Queue design: why separate queues (High / Normal / Low) are needed instead of a single FIFO queue.
Detail the Deduplication strategy: using Redis key with TTL `dedup:{userId}:{hash(template,params)}`.
Address failure recovery, dead-letter queues (DLQ), and retry exponential backoff.
hints: If marketing notifications and OTPs share the same Kafka topic/queue, a marketing blast of 10M emails will back up the queue, delaying 2FA OTP codes for hours.
Store user preferences and device tokens in a low-latency cache (Redis) with write-through / cache-aside to database.
alternativeApproaches: Using Temporal.io / AWS Step Functions for complex multi-step delivery workflows (e.g. "Send push; if unread after 10m, send SMS").
commonMistakes: Sending external emails/SMS synchronously inside the web request handler, locking client threads.
Using a single queue: marketing blasts drown out password resets and payment confirmation emails.
